absent: Numeric values of taskstats and cgroupstats command, attribute, and type identifiers, version constants, cpumask maximum length, and register versus deregister actions.
Full layouts of taskstats, cgroupstats, listener, per-CPU listener array, generic netlink info and message structures, and task and signal structures beyond touched fields.

Behavior of helpers only called but not routed here, including per-process fill, per-task add, reply sizing and sending, CPU list parsing, namespace accessors, and task lookup and signal-hand locking.
Cgroup statistics builder behavior and the meaning of its return codes.

Semantics of torture helpers only referenced here, including the common nanosecond sleep, random state and generator, stop and shutdown absorption, thread stopping, online CPU counting, and CPU add and remove.
Configuration sources and defaults for torture intervals, holdoffs, verbosity, type string, shutdown deadline and hook, stutter parameters, and on-off callback.
Scheduling normal helper semantics and allowed niceness bounds.
Accounting integral updater behavior and the units of user and system times.
User-count structure layout, reference counting rules, and hash-long behavior.

findings.text: Task and cgroup statistics are served through one generic netlink family with two get operations. The task operation requires administrative permission while the cgroup operation does not carry that flag in these fragments. Both operations disable strict and dump validation and bound attributes by their policy size. The family is marked network-namespace aware and reserves operation numbers above the cgroup get command.

The task statistics command selects a single handler by which attribute is present, with registration checked before deregistration, then per-process query, then per-thread-group query. Presence of the cpumask registration or deregistration attribute routes to a cpumask helper with the corresponding action. Presence of the process or thread-group identifier routes to the matching query helper. Absence of all known attributes is rejected.

The cgroup statistics command requires a file descriptor attribute, rejects an empty file reference, prepares a reply sized for one cgroup statistics record, reserves the record attribute, zeroes it, asks a builder to fill it from the descriptor path entry, and sends the reply. Failures during reply preparation, reservation, or building release the reply buffer and propagate a negative error.

Thread-group statistics start from the group leader stored signal statistics when present and otherwise from zero, then accumulate contributions only from non-exiting member threads using a single timestamp taken after the base copy, and finally stamp a version field. Lookup failure or inability to acquire the signal-hand lock yields a search error without producing data.

Thread-group aggregation runs under read-side RCU protection for task lookup and holds the target signal-hand lock while copying the base record and walking member threads, releasing the signal-hand lock before exiting RCU. The version stamp and return occur after both protections are released.

Listener registration validates that the requested mask is within possible CPUs and that caller user and process-ID namespaces are the initial ones. Per-CPU listener lists are each guarded by a dedicated read-write semaphore held for writing during insert, duplicate scan, and removal. A second valid registration for the same identifier on the same CPU is ignored rather than duplicated.

Cpumask text parsing rejects inputs above a maximum length and inputs shorter than one byte with distinct errors, duplicates the attribute payload into temporary storage, delegates interpretation to a CPU list parser, frees the temporary copy, and returns the parser result including allocation failure.

Early initialization creates a slab cache for task statistics records and initializes every possible CPU listener list head and semaphore. Later initialization registers the generic netlink family, records successful registration in a flag, and logs the family version. Registration failure aborts without setting the flag.

Torture shutdown coordination uses three modes for normal operation, system shutdown with torture active, and normal module removal, starting in removal mode. A shutdown notifier takes a dedicated mutex and moves normal operation to shutdown mode, while any other transition attempt under shutdown or removal only warns about concurrent removal and shutdown.

Offline attempts are ignored for already offline or non-hotpluggable CPUs and for the last remaining online CPU. Otherwise an attempt counter is incremented, removal is tried, and on success a success counter, accumulated duration, and running minimum and maximum durations are updated and a shared online estimate is decremented with a warning if it reaches zero or below. Boot-time busy failures can be forgiven without counting as attempts.

Online attempts are ignored for already online or non-hotpluggable CPUs. Otherwise an attempt counter is incremented, addition is tried, and on success a success counter, accumulated duration, and running minimum and maximum durations are updated and a shared online estimate is incremented. Boot-time busy failures can be forgiven without counting as attempts.

The on-off torture thread brings all possible CPUs online initially, disables itself when only CPU zero exists, optionally waits a holdoff interval, waits for kernel boot completion, then until asked to stop picks a random CPU within the observed maximum and tries offline with online as fallback, pausing between iterations. It can pause during boot when configured, and always restores all CPUs online before exiting.

Shuffle tracking links registered torture threads through a list node holding a task pointer. Global state comprises a head for that list, a dedicated mutex, a temporary CPU mask, an identifier for one CPU to leave idle, a shuffler thread pointer, and an interval controlling how often placement is reconsidered.

Registration of a thread for shuffling appends under the shuffle mutex. Each shuffle pass holds the CPU read lock and the shuffle mutex, does nothing when only one CPU is online, otherwise advances the idled CPU with wrap to none, and applies the resulting mask to registered threads either always or randomly depending on configuration.

Shuffle initialization stores the requested interval, clears the idled CPU marker, allocates a temporary mask, and starts a shuffler thread. Mask allocation failure is reported without starting the thread, and thread creation failure releases the mask.

The shutdown torture thread waits until an absolute deadline or a stop request, optionally reporting remaining time while waiting interruptibly. On stop it announces stopping and exits. On deadline expiry it clears its own task pointer to avoid self-join, runs an optional hook, optionally dumps tracing state, and powers the system off.

The stutter thread repeatedly publishes a near-future active deadline when a positive stutter length above one is configured, waits most of that window, then waits a gap interval, absorbing shutdown requests each cycle until asked to stop. Both waits are skipped appropriately when stopping.

Torture thread creation announces an informational message, creates a named kernel thread, reports a distinct error message and clears the output pointer on failure, otherwise runs an optional per-thread callback, wakes the thread, registers it for CPU shuffling, and returns success. Thread stopping is tolerant of a null pointer, otherwise announces, stops, and clears the pointer.

Setting torture thread scheduling priority clamps the requested niceness into the allowed minimum-maximum range with one-time warnings on each bound violation, then applies normal scheduling with the clamped value.

High-resolution torture sleeps convert microsecond, millisecond, jiffy, and second bases to nanoseconds and delegate to a common nanosecond routine in relative mode with caller-provided randomness state. Millisecond and second fuzz conversions saturate at the maximum unsigned 32-bit value on overflow, while the microsecond and jiffy forms use direct scaling.

Verbose throttling sleeps only when both frequency and duration are positive and an atomically incremented shared counter reaches a multiple of the frequency, sleeping uninterruptibly for the configured duration.

The initial user-count object binds the initial user namespace with the global root identity and a reference count of one. The hash table size is one shifted by a bit count, every bucket starts as an empty nulls list, and the hash mixes the numeric user identifier with the namespace address reduced by the same bit count.
A dedicated spinlock guards the user-count hash table, defined alongside the table storage.
CPU time accounting for a task forwards its current user and system times to an integral updater.
The shared online CPU estimate and the torture start time in jiffies are each exposed through a single-read accessor that returns the current stored value without further computation.

Listener registration can partially succeed across CPUs when allocation fails; the failure path removes any already inserted entries for the same identifier over the requested mask before returning the error. Reply construction for process, thread-group, and cgroup queries frees the in-progress message on size, reservation, fill, or build failures.

Hotplug torture never leaves the system with zero online CPUs from its own offline path and warns if its internal estimate reaches zero, forgives boot-time busy errors that would otherwise pollute statistics, and unconditionally re-onlines all possible CPUs on thread start and exit. Shuffle registration warns and drops null tasks or allocation failures instead of corrupting the list.
Fullstop modes have numeric values zero for continued operation, one for shutdown with torture active, and two for normal module removal.
Torture pseudo-random parameters are multiplier 39916801, addend 479001701, and refresh interval 10000.
Accounting size units define one kilobyte as 1024 bytes, one megabyte as 1024 kilobytes, and a mask that clears the low ten bits to round down to a kilobyte boundary.
User-count hash sizing uses ten bits, yielding 1024 buckets.

Torture initial values observed are verbose sleep duration one, offline and online minima negative one, shared online estimate starting at the compile-time possible CPU count, fullstop starting in removal mode, and shuffle idle marker set to negative one during shuffle initialization.

The cpumask attribute helper allocates a temporary mask, parses the selected attribute into it, and on success forwards the caller port identifier with the mask and requested action to the listener manager, propagating allocation or parse errors.

Process and thread-group queries each size a reply for one statistics record, prepare a new-command reply, extract the numeric identifier from its attribute, reserve a typed record, fill it from live state, and send the reply, freeing the message on any failure.
Torture logging uses an identity message prefix, a global type string prepended to diagnostics, and an integer verbosity level gating normal and detailed messages.

Hotplug torture keeps global attempt and success counts, accumulated durations, and running minima and maxima separately for offline and online directions, an optional callback run after each successful offline, and a pointer holding the on-off thread.

The shuffler thread starts by announcing, then until asked to stop waits the configured interval, reapplies CPU placement across registered threads, and absorbs shutdown requests, announcing stopping on exit.
The statistics netlink family object is marked read-only after initialization.
